segments.text: You've probably noticed by now that AI makes mistakes.
It can deliver incorrect facts, write a joke that falls completely flat, or build a complex
project plan that fails on day one, all with the exact same confident tone.
But pretending this technology doesn't exist isn't a realistic option.
The tool is entirely too powerful to leave sitting on the shelf.
To safely harness that power, you need to develop a specific set of skills.
You have to learn how to actively evaluate the results you get so you can remain smarter than the
tool you are using. Every time you hit enter on a prompt, you need to ask two core questions
of the result. Is the information factually right, and is it actually good enough for what I need to
accomplish? This flowchart outlines a three-step evaluation process for any prompt result. Step
one is performing a quick baseline review. Step two requires a closer look if the situation demands
it. Finally, step three forces a decision on what to do with the answer.
Applying these three steps allows you to extract the raw speed and brainstorming power of the AI
without inheriting any of its hidden errors. Let's break down that first phase.
No matter how simple the prompt, every single AI output requires a baseline check before you
put it to work. The quick review process starts with reading the answer in full. If you pass an
AI's text along, you personally own it. Quick review ends with deciding on a path forward based
on three options. If an AI's answer is accurate, you can publish it immediately, or give it to others
to use. However, you should still include a reference noting that you used AI to help with
the writing. If the results look like they are right, but you need to be sure, that's when you
move to step two. Next, understand the text to accurately judge it. Finally, validate the
output against your constraints, scanning from missing information or obvious factual errors.
For straightforward tasks with minimal consequences, a pass through these three basic checks is often
all you need to safely move forward. But if your unsure answer is correct, or if the consequences
of being wrong are high, you have to dig deeper. This take a closer look graphic shows how to assess
the situation. First, evaluate the tasks needs. A historical essay needs facts, while an email
needs polite writing. Next, evaluate the stakes. A movie pick is trivial, but medical advice carries
serious weight. The governing rule is simple. The more that depends on the answer being right,
the more carefully you must check the work. For deep dives, start by checking the sources.
Open the AI's links to verify they reliably support the claims. You can also challenge the
answer, asking the AI for arguments against its own conclusion. Finally, check it yourself by
running the math, testing code, or consulting an expert. By matching your level of scrutiny to
the potential risk of the task, you prevent critical failures from slipping into your most
important projects. Once you have evaluated the output, the process isn't over until you make
a definitive decision on how to utilize or discard that material. For the final phase,
you have three options. First, use it if the answer meets your standards.
Second, fix it by telling the AI what to change or making manual edits. Just remember to re-review.
Third, walk away. If the AI hallucinates or struggles, abandon the approach entirely.
Actively deciding the fate of an AI answer ensures you are directing the workflow,
rather than acting as a passive recipient of whatever the machine spits out. The foundational
dynamic between human and machine always comes back to this single rule. The tool generates the
answers, but you evaluate them. Review the initial output, take a closer look when the stakes are high,
and confidently decide your next step. By rigorously testing the information you receive,
you guarantee that the final product remains entirely your own.
